notes.bp: Bandwidth extension must recreate missing high-frequency speech without inventing spectral detail that listeners hear as distortion.
notes.wh: The missing band is not directly supervised by the degraded input; spectral errors can raise objective quality scores while changing consonant detail.
notes.naive: Copy low-frequency structure upward with a generic network and judge it by one waveform metric.
notes.ap: Use frequency-domain enhancement with an ICCRN-style recurrent representation to preserve global spectral structure while reconstructing the absent band.
notes.mech: The model operates on frequency representations, combines local and global context, and is compared against EBEN and other bandwidth-extension baselines.
notes.math: PESQ, SI-SDR, STOI, and MUSHRA separate signal fidelity, intelligibility, and listener preference.
notes.dots: Bandwidth extension is an inverse problem: plausible high frequencies are constrained by the observed band and perceptual targets, not uniquely recovered.
notes.ww: The tests show gains over the original EBEN, including a 40-person MUSHRA comparison; the authors report clearer high-frequency detail and less distortion.
notes.limits: French LibriSpeech, sampling setup, listeners, and author-reported metrics bound the result; other languages remain open.

notes.bp: Brain recordings may contain enough motor or auditory information to reconstruct intelligible speech for people who cannot produce it normally.
notes.wh: Neural signals are indirect, data are limited, and a reconstruction can be spectrally plausible yet unintelligible or unnatural.
notes.naive: Map neural features directly to a waveform and let a generic vocoder repair phase and prosody.
notes.ap: Separate linguistic/prosodic prediction from neural phase reconstruction, then use a neural vocoder and a learned MOSA evaluator.
notes.mech: MiSTR uses a multimodal iEEG encoder, Transformer spectrogram/prosody prediction, and a neural phase vocoder with adaptive spectral correction.
notes.math: Mel-spectrogram correlation, intelligibility, naturalness, and MOSA expose different reconstruction failures; MOSA is reported at 3.38.
notes.dots: The system is a chain of constrained reconstructions: neural evidence determines content and prosody while the vocoder supplies waveform detail.
notes.ww: The paper reports higher fidelity and naturalness than listed baselines and MOSA 3.38.
notes.limits: Dataset, subjects, protocol, learned evaluator, and paper-reported comparisons limit clinical claims.

notes.bp: Audio-text classifiers fail when the acoustic domain changes even if the label vocabulary stays fixed.
notes.wh: The text embedding can remain stable while the audio embedding moves with background and SNR.
notes.naive: Tune only text prompts or assume a frozen audio-text embedding is domain invariant.
notes.ap: Adapt the audio side using representative target-domain sound examples and test transfer across environments.
notes.mech: The method aligns audio representations to the target domain and compares audio-based with text-based adaptation.
notes.math: Top-1 accuracy across environments and SNRs measures whether adaptation closes the modality/domain gap; the zero-shot reference is 32.4%.
notes.dots: Domain adaptation changes which acoustic evidence the shared representation treats as invariant while preserving the open label interface.
notes.ww: Audio-based adaptation gives the largest reported gains across tested conditions.
notes.limits: Sound set, target examples, class construction, and reported accuracy limit open-world claims.

notes.bp: Listeners combine segmental sounds and lexical pitch accent when recognizing Japanese words, even when the cues disagree.
notes.wh: The cues arrive together, priming can mask later effects, and response time does not by itself identify the updated representation.
notes.naive: Treat phonemes as the only lexical evidence or assume prosody simply overrides segments.
notes.ap: Create controlled incongruent words and use repetition priming and response timing to test each cue.
notes.mech: Experiments isolate cue type, delay, and lexical repetition; mixed-effects models compare segmental and prosodic conditions.
notes.math: Response-time models compare conditions; the paper reports prosodic inhibition at a 750 ms interval.
notes.dots: Prosody is part of lexical recognition, not only an expression-layer signal.
notes.ww: Results suggest prosodic mispronunciation inhibits recognition at the tested delay.
notes.limits: Japanese materials, pitch-accent system, participants, and laboratory task limit cross-language generalization.

notes.bp: Personalized TTS for dysarthric speakers must preserve identity while producing intelligible speech from scarce and errorful recordings.
notes.wh: A model can improve intelligibility by erasing the speaker traits personalization is meant to retain.
notes.naive: Fine-tune directly on all target audio and accept overfitting or poor pronunciation.
notes.ap: Anchor the target speaker to a teacher model and use curriculum learning before specializing to dysarthric articulation.
notes.mech: A teacher-student knowledge-anchoring framework is evaluated across speaker groups with shortened audio.
notes.math: PER measures intelligibility and speaker similarity measures identity; reported PER reaches 15.579 and similarity rises from 0.586 to 0.708.
notes.dots: Personalization is constrained transfer: move toward the target voice without transferring articulation errors as content errors.
notes.ww: Curriculum and anchoring lower PER and improve speaker similarity across reported groups.
notes.limits: Groups, language, recording conditions, and reported metrics limit clinical claims.

notes.bp: ASR and humans should be compared on the same speech-in-noise task rather than assuming low WER means human-like hearing.
notes.wh: Human recognition depends on thresholds, spatial cues, rooms, and masking; model size changes errors without modeling those mechanisms.
notes.naive: Report ASR WER in clean speech as a proxy for hearing performance.
notes.ap: Estimate speech-reception thresholds from controlled sentences in noise for ASR models and humans.
notes.mech: Whisper models are tested on anechoic and spatial signals; thresholds come from WER curves at 50% error.
notes.math: SRT and psychometric slope make the human-machine gap explicit rather than hiding it in average WER.
notes.dots: Hearing is an operating boundary shaped by scene geometry and noise, not one recognition score.
notes.ww: Model size improves ASR thresholds, but the gap changes with language, room, and spatial signals.
notes.limits: Whisper versions, German/English material, steady noise, and laboratory setup limit claims.

notes.bp: A multilingual recognizer must allocate limited capacity across languages with different data sizes and acoustic demands.
notes.wh: Average scores hide low-resource failures; language-ID errors and subword choices can contaminate recognition.
notes.naive: Train one pooled recognizer and optimize aggregate CER, letting high-resource languages dominate.
notes.ap: Use hybrid language identification, multilingual and language-specific models, and targeted decoding resources.
notes.mech: The system combines language identification with multilingual ASR and customized models, then evaluates language ID and CER.
notes.math: Language-ID accuracy and mean CER expose routing and transcription separately; reported values are 86.8% and 27.4%.
notes.dots: Multilinguality is resource allocation: the front end decides the linguistic regime before recognition specializes.
notes.ww: The system is competitive with challenge baselines and identifies languages needing targeted work.
notes.limits: Challenge data, language mix, averaging, and tuning limit all-multilingual claims.

notes.bp: ASR robustness should be tested on errors people actually produce, not only clean speech or synthetic noise.
notes.wh: Speech errors differ by type and position; aggregate WER hides which deviation caused failure.
notes.naive: Report one WER on spontaneous speech and treat all deviations as equivalent noise.
notes.ap: Use annotated SFUSED speech errors to stratify WhisperX performance by error type and word position.
notes.mech: The study evaluates sound and word errors with controlled classification variables and compares initial, medial, and final positions.
notes.math: Accuracy by error class and position reveals interactions; sound errors are reported as easier than word errors.
notes.dots: Robustness is a boundary map: which linguistic deviations cross the recognizer's failure boundary, and where.
notes.ww: Sound errors have higher transcription accuracy than word errors, with position-dependent differences.
notes.limits: Database, annotations, WhisperX, language, and task design limit generalization.
